section_summary: This section contains State Department press material, internal memoranda, cross-reference sheets, congressional correspondence, and a large body of public appeals concerning American exports of arms, raw materials, and aeronautical supplies to Japan during the war in China. Petitioners, legislators, missionaries, and religious and civic leaders pressed for the Coffee and Pittman measures, an embargo on war-sustaining trade, and changes to neutrality legislation; Department replies emphasized that no new arms-export licenses to Japan were being issued but that existing law did not restrict most raw materials. The section also documents diplomatic discussion of possible iron-ore restrictions and the Aluminum Corporation of America's adherence to the Department's voluntary policy against supplying Japanese aircraft production.

subfiles.title: Secretary Hull press-conference remarks on foreign affairs and proposed legislation affecting Japan
subfiles.about: Hull answers questions about General Marshall, Éamon de Valera, Senator Pittman's Japan bill, and the Mediterranean squadron.
subfiles.summary: Hull declines to comment authoritatively on a possible visit by General Marshall to Brazil and expresses regret over the reported cancellation of de Valera's visit. He says Pittman's bill concerning Japan and the Nine-Power Treaty is the senator's individual proposal and refers questions about the Mediterranean naval squadron to the Navy.

subfiles.title: Lyndon B. Johnson forwards R. M. Perrenot's letter
subfiles.about: Johnson asks Hull to consider and return a constituent's letter about American supplies reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Johnson encloses a letter from R. M. Perrenot of Austin, Texas, and asks that Perrenot's views receive careful consideration. He also requests that the constituent letter be returned for his files.

subfiles.title: R. M. Perrenot protests American assistance to Japan
subfiles.about: Perrenot urges congressional action to stop American materials from supporting Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Perrenot condemns reports that the United States supplies a large share of Japan's war materials and quotes an American doctor who treated Chinese victims wounded by American scrap iron and shell fragments. He calls the trade a national disgrace and asks Johnson to use his influence to end it.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Johnson concerning Perrenot's protest
subfiles.about: Hull provides the Department's position on exports to China and Japan and returns Perrenot's letter.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses a Department statement and recalls the July 1938 moral embargo on aeronautical supplies for countries bombing civilian populations. He reports that no arms-export licenses for Japan had been sought or issued in the preceding three months and says shipments under older licenses would soon cease.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on discouraging a French approach over Philippine iron ore
subfiles.about: The memorandum proposes discouraging a French request that the United States halt Philippine iron-ore shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Division notes a Paris telegram suggesting that France might approach Washington about cutting off iron ore from the Philippines to Japan. It recommends invoking considerations previously explained by Moffat to Mallet, while observing that the British had earlier said they had successfully discouraged the proposal.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Paris to discourage the proposed approach on iron supplies
subfiles.about: The Department authorizes the embassy to discourage an approach concerning restrictions on iron supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Responding to telegram 874, the Department asks the embassy, at its discretion, to discourage the proposed approach in appropriate French quarters. The embassy is directed to cite the considerations in the penultimate paragraph of instruction 1455 of May 1.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Bullitt's telegram on stopping iron shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a telegram about possible cessation of iron shipments from French Indochina, British Malaya, and the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: The reference identifies telegram 874 from Bullitt in France. It records comments made in a conversation with Jean Chauvel concerning iron shipments to Japan from three Asian territories.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Senator Donahey's inquiry about moving a company branch to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to an inquiry about relocating the Wooster branch of United Engineering and Foundry Company to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced letter concerns moving the company's Wooster, Ohio branch to Japan. It also requests information about establishing branches of American businesses elsewhere in the world.

subfiles.title: Petition declaration for non-participation in Japanese aggression
subfiles.about: The petition calls for legislation condemning Japan and barring Japanese purchases of materials useful in warfare.
subfiles.summary: The declaration accuses Japan of bombing civilians, violating treaties, and using American commerce to sustain its campaign in China. It asks Congress to confirm Japan's treaty violations, condemn Japanese military practices, and close American markets to Japanese purchases of war-useful materials.

subfiles.title: American Committee report and appeal to Secretary Hull
subfiles.from: Elizabeth Rugh Price, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The committee reports a nationwide petition campaign and urges embargo legislation directed at Japan.
subfiles.summary: The committee reports 620 petitions containing about 391,000 signatures, together with actions by numerous civic, church, and veterans' organizations. It urges support for Representative Coffee's embargo resolution and opposes the Pittman cash-and-carry measure unless the Far East is excluded and Japanese purchases are separately restricted. A state-by-state summary details the geographic reach of the campaign.

subfiles.title: American Committee report and appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Elizabeth Rugh Price, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The committee informs Roosevelt of nationwide protests against American participation in Japan's war on China.
subfiles.summary: The letter repeats that 620 petitions carry approximately 391,000 signatures and that many large organizations have taken official action. It links Japan to the Rome-Berlin Axis and asks Roosevelt to give the Far Eastern situation full consideration. The accompanying state-by-state summary includes an Oklahoma entry not present in the copy sent to Hull.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Mrs. Price
subfiles.about: Moore acknowledges the committee's letters to Roosevelt and Hull concerning embargo and neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: The Department summarizes the committee's support for the Coffee resolution and its objections to the Pittman measure unless the Far East is exempted. Moore thanks Price for writing both the President and Secretary of State and promises careful consideration.

subfiles.title: John H. Cowles advocates stronger international action and the Coffee Bill
subfiles.about: Cowles argues against isolationism and supports legislation that would restrict aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cowles praises American intervention in the First World War and argues that moral support for Britain and France might have prevented the Munich settlement. He endorses the Coffee Bill and says the Pittman resolutions could be acceptable if amended so that China, rather than Japan, benefited in the Pacific.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to John H. Cowles
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Cowles's views on neutrality legislation and foreign affairs.
subfiles.summary: Moore thanks Cowles for his May 9 letter. He assures him that his views on neutrality legislation and related foreign-policy questions will receive careful attention.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Peck's discussion with China's foreign minister
subfiles.about: The sheet references a telegram reporting Chinese questions about Hull's neutrality testimony.
subfiles.summary: The referenced conversation was between Mr. Peck and China's minister of foreign affairs. The minister commented on and inquired about the Secretary of State's testimony before a Senate committee concerning neutrality legislation.

subfiles.title: Roosevelt's memorandum requesting a reply to Bishop Oldham
subfiles.about: Roosevelt asks the Department to answer Bishop Oldham's attached letter.
subfiles.summary: The President forwards Bishop Oldham's communication to the Department of State. He requests that the Department prepare and send a reply.

subfiles.title: Bishop Oldham urges an end to war-material trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Oldham supports the Pittman and Coffee proposals and calls for revision of American neutrality policy.
subfiles.summary: Oldham describes trade in war materials with Japan as immoral and dangerous and supports the Pittman resolution, Coffee Bill, and Thomas Amendment. He argues that preventing war internationally offers a better means of keeping America out of war than isolationism and says his views are widely shared by his clergy and community.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Bishop Oldham
subfiles.about: Moore acknowledges Oldham's views and explains the Department's policy toward arms and aeronautical exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Writing at Roosevelt's request, Moore thanks Oldham and says informed public views are considered in foreign-policy formulation. He recounts the moral embargo on aeronautical supplies and reports that no new licenses for arms, ammunition, or implements of war to Japan had been issued during the preceding three months.

subfiles.title: Robert Hall Glover urges broader restrictions on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Glover argues that raw-material sales still support Japan's military industry and advocates new legislation.
subfiles.summary: Glover welcomes the absence of recent arms-export licenses but stresses that Japan continues to receive American materials used in domestic munitions production. He urges prompt passage of the new Pittman resolution and Coffee Bill and opposes the Peace Act of 1939 unless the Far East is excluded and Japanese purchases are separately stopped.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Robert Hall Glover
subfiles.about: Moore acknowledges Glover's views on Japanese exports and pending neutrality bills.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes Glover's reference to earlier correspondence about war-material exports to Japan. Moore thanks him for his discussion of neutrality measures before Congress and promises careful attention.

subfiles.title: Wirt W. Hallam writes Hull on the costs of supplying Japan
subfiles.about: Hallam argues that American war-material exports to Japan have produced greater defense, relief, and trade losses for the United States.
subfiles.summary: Hallam estimates that roughly $600 million in war materials sold to Japan has helped create billions of dollars in American defense, charitable, and commercial costs. He calls for an end to war-equipment shipments, expanded aid for China's sick, wounded, and refugees, and consideration of a larger loan to China.
keywords: American Association for China Famine and Flood Relief

subfiles.title: Wirt W. Hallam writes Roosevelt on the costs of supplying Japan
subfiles.about: Hallam sends Roosevelt substantially the same economic and humanitarian argument previously addressed to Hull.
subfiles.summary: Hallam contends that sales to Japan strengthen a potential Pacific adversary while destroying American trade in China and Manchuria. He proposes stopping war-equipment exports, aiding Chinese victims, and making a larger loan to China as an alternative to greater coastal-defense expenditure.

subfiles.title: Yost acknowledges Hallam's White House letter
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the May 19 letter referred by the White House and points to the Department's earlier response.
subfiles.summary: Yost confirms receipt through the White House of Hallam's letter about the Far Eastern situation. He refers Hallam to the Department's May 24 answer to the similar letter of May 16.

subfiles.title: Yost replies to Hallam's May 16 letter
subfiles.about: Yost explains current export policy and describes private American relief for China.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses the Department's statement and explains the moral embargo on aeronautical supplies and the absence of new arms-export licenses to Japan during the preceding four months. He adds that the American Red Cross and other private organizations are assisting Chinese noncombatants and that Red Cross appropriations and collections for China exceeded $800,000.

subfiles.title: Senator Capper asks whether the United States is aiding Japan
subfiles.about: Capper quotes constituent protests and asks whether American trade is materially assisting Japan's war effort.
subfiles.summary: Capper quotes missionary George E. Lerrigo, who connects American supplies with the bombing of Chongqing, and Mrs. Floyd Souders, who cites Charles P. Culver's account of the war in China. The letters distinguish formal arms exports from continued sales of scrap iron, gasoline, oil, and other raw materials, and Capper asks whether the charge of American aid to Japan is factually justified.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Senator Capper on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Hull answers Capper's May 16 and 17 inquiries and explains the legal limits on export controls.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses copies of the Department's export statement and says existing law permits restrictions only on defined arms, ammunition, implements of war, tin-plate scrap, and helium gas. Other commodities remain freely exportable, although manufacturers are complying with the moral embargo on aeronautical supplies and no new arms licenses for Japan had been issued during the preceding four months. Blackburn's letter is returned with the reply.

subfiles.title: Senator Capper forwards Robert J. Blackburn's protest
subfiles.about: Capper forwards another Kansas constituent's protest against perceived American partiality toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Capper refers to his previous letter about George Lerrigo and Mrs. Floyd Souders. He encloses Robert J. Blackburn's similar protest so that it can be considered with the other Kansas correspondence.

subfiles.title: Robert J. Blackburn urges an end to war-sustaining trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Blackburn asks Capper to support legislation ending trade that sustains Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: Blackburn argues that American munitions and supplies help Japan gain control of China and threaten future American access to Chinese markets. He also commends Capper's support for the Ludlow Amendment as a genuine peace measure.

subfiles.title: Florida secretary of state transmits legislative memorials to Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Gray forwards certified copies of two memorials adopted by the 1939 Florida Legislature.
subfiles.summary: Florida Secretary of State R. A. Gray transmits Senate Joint Memorial No. 1 and Senate Memorial No. 3 at the legislature's direction. The following pages reproduce the memorial concerning sales of munitions and war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Florida Senate Memorial No. 3 against sales of war materials to Japan
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: The Florida Legislature memorializes federal officials to terminate American sales of munitions and war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The resolution declares that ending Japan's ability to buy munitions and war materials would deny assistance to its war against China. It asks Florida's congressional delegation to support appropriate legislation and directs distribution of copies to federal leaders. The governor approved it on May 10, it was filed on May 11, and R. A. Gray certified the copy on May 12.

subfiles.title: Referral slip for the Arkansas petition correspondence
subfiles.about: A largely illegible routing sheet refers the attached China petition correspondence to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: The slip bears file number 894.24/666 and a May 20 receipt marking. Its surviving text indicates that the accompanying material was respectfully referred for departmental handling.

subfiles.title: Senator Caraway forwards a Bentonville petition to Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Caraway sends Roosevelt a China petition received from Mrs. C. M. Armstrong of Bentonville, Arkansas.
subfiles.summary: Caraway encloses the petition at Armstrong's request. She states that it is being submitted simply for the President's information.

subfiles.title: Bentonville petition demanding an end to war supplies for Japan
subfiles.from: C. M. Armstrong, E. M. Armstrong, and other Bentonville petitioners
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and members of Congress
subfiles.about: Arkansas petitioners demand immediate action to stop American war supplies from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: The petitioners contend that the United States violates at least the spirit of neutrality by supplying Japan while Japan avoids a formal declaration of war against China. Invoking humanity and Christianity, they ask federal officials to halt further war supplies. The second page consists mainly of difficult-to-read signatures.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Aluminum Corporation requests from Mitsui and Mitsubishi
subfiles.about: Yost records the Aluminum Corporation of America's decision to continue refusing aeronautical materials requested for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Wilbur reports that Mitsui and Mitsubishi requested quotations for piston and impeller forgings after the Aluminum Corporation had stopped supplying Japanese aircraft uses. Yost confirms that the Department's policy remains unchanged, and Wilbur indicates that the company will refuse to quote. Wilbur also reports that Japan is obtaining most aircraft aluminum from Germany, while French buyers still prefer American material.
